newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Winterthur convinced about '96 fin result.
newsitem.headline: Winterthur convinced about '96 fin result.

text.p: Winterthur Insurance Co said it was convinced that it would be able to achieve another excellent financial result this year, but added that it was cautious about the Swiss market.

Investment income in the first half of 2.78 billion Swiss francs was more or less in line with the budget, which foresees an increase of eight to 10 percent, Erwin Heri, head of Winterthur's finance department, told a news conference.
Heri said his confidence about full-year results were based on a calming down of financial markets since a shake-up in July and the return of exchange rates to mid-year levels.
"Naturally, this forecast is subject to any crashes in the global markets during the next few months," Heri added.
Winterthur had also become cautious about its assessment of the Swiss equity market, which contributes to the largest share of its portfolio.

First of all, Heri said, the Swiss market was no longer cheap and secondly the economy had remained subdued and that would affect equity markets sooner or later. Thirdly, the market had already showed signs of these effects, even if not overtly.
Heri said the broad Swiss market index SMI had risen only 3.3 percent in the first nine months of this year, excluding Novartis shares, Ciba-Geigy AG and Sandoz AG.
Including Novartis, the SMI had risen 12.0 percent, he said.
Among the reasons for Heri's moderate optimism was improving economic trends in Switzerland's trading partners, mainly Germany, and the decline in short-term rates by the Swiss National Bank (SNB).
Heri said last week's cut in the Swiss discount rate to 1.00 percent was a good sign and money market rates could probably have room to fall a little further.
The only real change in Winterthur's investment portfolio during the first half of 1996 was a relative decline in bonds in favour of loans and money market investments.

The amount of stocks in its portfolio had also risen, but Heri said this was in line with Winterthur's long-term strategy. Investments in stocks had risen to the current level of 16.8 percent from 14 percent at the end of 1994.
The rise in stocks was to a large extent from Winterthur companies outside Switzerland, which still had low stock allocations, Heri said.
Winterthur, however, had become rather cautious about the Swiss equity portfolios, also because it believed it now had the strategically correct allocation.
"In this, we have even gone as far as to hedge part of the exposure in the Swiss equity market, thus reducing our exposure by about a third," Heri said.
At the end of June, Winterthur had total investments of 78.3 billion Swiss francs of which bonds accounted for 37.6 percent, down from 38.3 percent at the end of 1995.
The decline in bonds was partially because Winterthur was replacing bonds in Germany with liquid and higher yielding marketable loans, so-called "Schuldscheindarlehen."

Heri also said that Winterthur had started replacing Swiss bonds in its portfolio with foreign currency bonds of those countries, such as Germany, which had interest differentials of 200 basis points or more and had a currency undervalued against the Swiss franc.

"...it should be noted that yields on government bonds in Switzerland, which have since again fallen 4.00 percent, are simply not attractive enough for investors to buy large amounts of such bonds," Heri said.
